newsitem.title: USA: Sears to refund payments of certain debtors.
newsitem.headline: Sears to refund payments of certain debtors.

text.p: Sears, Roebuck and Co. said Thursday it would refund money collected from some credit card debtors who declared bankruptcy and made repayment agreements with Sears that the nation's No. 2 retailer now says were improper.
Sears said the plan, which covers repayment agreements going back to 1992, could have a material effect on 1997 earnings but also said it was in the early stages of assessing the plan's cost.

The Hoffman Estates, Ill.-based retailer's stock dropped $3, or more than 5 percent, to $47.75 in early afternoon trading on the New York Stock Exchange, where it was one of the most actively traded shares.

Sears outlined the plan in a filing with U.S. Bankruptcy Court in Boston. The company said it had received documents related to the issues involved and stemming from a class-action lawsuit filed with the court.

The refunds involve certain credit card debtors who filed for Chapter 7 bankruptcy, Sears said. The credit card holders filed for bankruptcy but arranged a payment plan -- or "debt reaffirmation" -- with Sears, a company spokesman said.
But the debt reaffirmations were not filed as required under the Bankruptcy Code, Sears said.

Debt reaffirmations allow a debtor who is filing for bankruptcy to make payments to some creditors in an effort to preserve his or her credit standing. Debt reaffirmations must be filed with the bankruptcy court to be valid.
Sears said it had exercised "flawed legal judgment" in the execution and handling of some of the agreements.
It said senior management last week directed that all reaffirmations must be filed in a timely fashion, and that on Wednesday it launched a voluntary plan to refund payments made by some debtors.

Under the plan, Sears will return funds collected under reaffirmation agreements that were not filed with the bankruptcy court, including principal and finance charges with interest, the retailer said.
The company plans to identify debtors whose reaffirmation agreements were not properly filed from 1992 until now, the company said.
Until repayments can be made, Sears will cease sending billing statements and assessing interest charges to former debtors who signed the reaffirmation agreements in question.
It said it has discussed its plan with the Massachusetts attorney general's office and the U.S. Bankruptcy Trustee for Region 1, which includes Massachusetts.
Sears also said it had retained the services of a New York University law school professor to review its reaffirmation agreement procedures.
Sears, the nation's second-ranking retailer after Wal-Mart Stores Inc., had profits of $567 million, or $1.42 per share, on revenues of $12 billion in 1996.
